core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Intermittent Palpitations is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes assessing red flags, obtaining an ECG and labs, reducing caffeine intake, considering ambulatory monitoring, and safety-netting for syncope or chest pain, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodes of palpitations for 3 weeks
Key HPI features: sudden episodes of fast heartbeat lasting 5-10 minutes, sometimes with lightheadedness, triggered by coffee and stress, no chest pain or syncope
Objective/Exam findings: Check pulse, BP, ECG, thyroid function, FBC, electrolytes. Consider Holter monitor.
Relevant background/PMH: no known medical problems
Current medications: combined oral contraceptive pill, no supplements
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Intermittent Palpitations.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Supraventricular tachycardia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Palpitations with fainting, chest pain, or a family history of sudden death.
management_principles: Assess red flags, ECG, labs, reduce caffeine, consider ambulatory monitoring, safety-net for syncope/chest pain
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients with Supraventricular Tachycardia

reference_soap.objective: Check pulse, BP, ECG, thyroid function, FBC, electrolytes. Consider Holter monitor.
reference_soap.assessment: Intermittent palpitations. DDx: SVT, premature beats, anxiety, hyperthyroidism, anaemia.
reference_soap.plan: Assess red flags, ECG, labs, reduce caffeine, consider ambulatory monitoring, safety-net for syncope/chest pain.

learning_objectives: Ask about rhythm symptoms, triggers, duration, syncope, chest pain

teaching.one_liner: The heart being felt when it normally isn't. The history — how it starts, stops, and feels — separates a benign cause from an arrhythmia.
red_flags: Palpitations with fainting, chest pain, or a family history of sudden death

must_ask.say: Does it start suddenly, like a switch, or build up gradually?
Could you tap out the rhythm for me? Is it regular or all over the place?
Is there anything that sets it off — caffeine, alcohol, exercise, stress?
Have you ever passed out or had chest pain with an episode?
Have you noticed weight loss, feeling hot, or trembling hands?

must_ask.objective: Family history of early heart disease
must_ask.say: Has anyone in your family had a heart attack, especially young?

history.answer: I've been having sudden episodes where my heart starts beating really fast, and it has been happening for the past three weeks.
It feels like my heart is fluttering and racing very fast inside my chest, like a hummingbird trapped inside.
It beats very fast but in a steady, regular rhythm, like tap-tap-tap-tap without skipping beats.
It starts completely out of nowhere like flipping an electric switch, and then it stops just as abruptly.
The episodes started three weeks ago, last about five to ten minutes each time, and happen two or three times a week.
They usually happen when I'm drinking my afternoon coffee or staying up late studying under exam stress.
Resting quietly and drinking a cold glass of water seem to help it go back to normal.
I've felt slightly lightheaded once or twice when it was racing, but I have never passed out, blacked out, or fainted.
No, it doesn't happen while I'm exercising or running; it usually hits when I'm sitting down studying.
No, I haven't had any chest pain, chest pressure, or shortness of breath during the episodes.
No, I haven't had any heat intolerance, excessive sweating, unintentional weight loss, or hand tremors.
No, I haven't felt unusually tired, my periods aren't heavy, and I haven't noticed any pale or yellow skin.
No, I haven't seen any black tarry stools or blood in my stool.
No, I don't get severe pounding headaches, cold drenching sweats, or pale skin during the episodes.
No, I don't feel shaky or sweaty when I miss a meal.
I feel stressed about my exams, but I haven't had sudden panic attacks, hyperventilation, or numbness in my hands.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, cough, sore throat, or recent viral infections.
I drink about three mugs of brewed coffee every day to stay awake for studying, but no energy drinks.
No, I don't take any cold syrups, nasal decongestant sprays, asthma inhalers, or diet pills.
I've never had high blood pressure, heart disease, or any abnormal heart tracings before.
No one in my family died suddenly at a young age, and there's no history of arrhythmias or heart muscle problems.
I've wondered if it's just exam anxiety, but it feels so physical that I worry it might be a true heart rhythm problem.
I wanted to see if I need an electrocardiogram or any medication to stop this from happening during my exams.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I've never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I take a combined oral contraceptive pill every morning, and I don't take any vitamins or herbal supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I drink alcohol occasionally, maybe a glass of wine once or twice a month with friends.
I'm a medical student studying for my board exams, and I live alone in an apartment near campus.
My last period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days on the pill, and there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Alert, calm, and appears comfortable in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute regular, respirations 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are clear and anicteric.
No exophthalmos, lid lag, or abnormal eye signs; pupils are equal and reactive.
Thyroid gland is normal size, symmetrical, non-tender, with no palpable nodules or bruits.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Radial pulses are strong, regular at 76 beats per minute, and symmetric bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds throughout both lung fields without crackles or wheezing.
No fine postural or resting tremor seen in the outstretched fingers.
No pretibial or pedal edema bilaterally.
